prompt: Inside the office, a reporting app hangs for about a minute whenever its database port is blocked, and users think it has crashed. The firewall team asks which rule action to use for that port on the internal network. What does the lesson recommend?

choices.text: Drop, so that a stranger scanning the network learns little about the machine
choices.why: That is why drop suits the internet side; inside, it leaves legitimate programs hanging.

choices.text: Reject with a TCP reset, so the app fails at once with a clear error
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Drop, and raise the app's timeout so the reply has time to arrive
choices.why: A dropped attempt gets no reply at any timeout; a longer wait only stretches the hang.

choices.text: Accept the port and let the database's own login turn away unwanted clients
choices.why: That removes the block altogether, which is not what the team asked for.

prompt: A branch office says file copies to head office crawl at a fraction of the line's speed, though pages do load in the end and nothing is reported down. On the Linux file server, which reading does the lesson take first?

choices.text: `nstat -az TcpRetransSegs`, to see whether segments are being resent
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: `ss -tan state time-wait`, since a pile of closed connections slows a server
choices.why: Thousands of TIME-WAIT lines mean a busy server, not a broken one.

choices.text: `ss -tulpn`, to confirm that the file service is still listening on its port
choices.why: The copies are running, so something is listening; the question is what happens to their packets.

choices.text: `dig` against both offices' resolvers, as slow transfers begin with slow names
choices.why: A name is looked up before the connection opens; it does not slow bytes already flowing.

prompt: After the three-way handshake, a client sends its first request: 512 bytes, starting at relative sequence number 1. Counting the way the lesson's capture does, what number does the server put in its `ack` for that request?

Your company runs the authoritative DNS for example.com on ns1. A partner's mail server complains that 192.0.2.80 gives no proper name when looked up backwards. Where does the `PTR` record for it get changed?

choices.text: With whoever holds that block of IPs, such as your provider
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: In the example.com zone on ns1, next to the A record for www
choices.why: The reverse name lives under in-addr.arpa, which follows the addresses, not your domain.

choices.text: In a TXT record on example.com, which partner mail servers read as the reverse name
choices.why: TXT carries rules such as SPF; a reverse lookup asks for a PTR under in-addr.arpa.

choices.text: At the registrar, which publishes the reverse name for each domain it sells
choices.why: A registrar sells the name; reverse zones belong to whoever owns the address block.

prompt: You add a record to the zone file on example.com's primary server and reload it; `dig @` the primary shows the record. Hours later the secondary server still answers from the old zone, and its log shows no transfer. What was most likely forgotten?

choices.text: Waiting out the record's TTL, after which the secondary asks again
choices.why: The TTL says how long resolvers may keep an answer, not when a secondary copies the zone.

choices.text: Running named-checkzone, which signals the new version of the zone to other servers
choices.why: named-checkzone checks the file for mistakes; it tells no other server anything.

choices.text: Raising the SOA serial number, which is how secondaries notice a change
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Flushing the resolver's cache with unbound-control so the secondary sees it
choices.why: That empties one resolver's copy; a secondary takes zone data from the primary, not from a resolver.

prompt: `tcpdump -e arp` showed two replies to one request for the file server's 192.168.10.10, and the MAC in the wrong one led you to a printer installed this morning with that number typed in by hand. After taking it off the printer, what keeps this from happening again?

choices.text: Flushing the neighbour table on each PC every morning with `ip neigh flush`
choices.why: Flushing only resets whom a PC believed; with two owners of one address the race starts again.

choices.text: Fixed devices get numbers outside the DHCP range, or a DHCP reservation
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Moving the file server to a switch port far from the one the printer uses
choices.why: Both are still on one network and both still answer the same ARP request.

choices.text: A rule on the router blocking ARP replies that come from printers
choices.why: ARP stays on the local network and is answered before any router sees it; the fix is in the addressing.

prompt: A capture was saved on the faulty machine with `tcpdump -w /tmp/web.pcap host 192.0.2.80`. To print it back later, with the same filters available, the command is `tcpdump -n ___ /tmp/web.pcap`.
From home you need a shell on www, which accepts SSH only from the office. A colleague's habit is `ssh -A office`, then `ssh www` from there. What does the lesson do instead, and why?

choices.text: `ssh -A` as suggested, since the agent keeps the key encrypted on the server
choices.why: With `-A`, whoever is root on the office server can use your agent while you are connected.

choices.text: Copy the private key to the office server, so the second hop needs no agent
choices.why: A private key stays on the machine it was made on; a copy on a server is a copy its root can take.

choices.text: `ssh -J office www`: the office server relays bytes, and your key stays home
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Ask for www's firewall to let your home address in, then use `ssh www` directly
choices.why: That widens a sensible rule to an address nobody else checks; the jump host keeps one door.

prompt: Ana runs `ssh -f -N -L 5432:10.0.0.7:5432 office` on her laptop. The database at 10.0.0.7 answers from the office server and is not reachable from the laptop. She then points her database client at `127.0.0.1:5432` on the laptop. What happens?

choices.text: It fails, because the laptop itself has no route to 10.0.0.7
choices.why: The destination in `-L` is seen from the server; the laptop talks only to its own port and to sshd.

choices.text: It reaches the laptop's own port 5432, where no database is listening
choices.why: ssh is listening on that port now, and carries whatever arrives there to the server.

choices.text: It connects: sshd on the office server opens the last leg to 10.0.0.7
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: It connects, and the database records the laptop's address as the client
choices.why: The last connection is made by sshd on the server, so the database sees the server.

prompt: On a Linux client, `cat /proc/sys/net/ipv4/ip_local_port_range` prints `32768   60999`, the range the kernel picks source ports from. At most how many connections can this client hold open at once to one server's address and port, from its single address?
The office server was reinstalled over the weekend, and `ssh office` now refuses with `WARNING: REMOTE HOST IDENTIFICATION HAS CHANGED!`. Put the steps in the order the lesson takes them.
items: Note the fingerprint the warning says the server sent
Read the server's own fingerprint with `ssh-keygen -lf` at its console
Connect again and accept the key, as on a first connection
trap: Removing the old line before comparing fingerprints turns an unexplained warning into a yes typed blind.

prompt: One ping crosses the office router, which also does NAT, and is captured on both of its sides. Match each part of the request to what the router did to it.

pairs.right: replaced, with a new pair for the next link
one lower than before the router
the same number on both sides
rewritten to the office's public address

right_distractors: raised by one at the router

prompt: A nightly backup runs over one TCP connection on a 1 Gbps link to a site 40 ms away, round trip. By the lesson's bandwidth-delay product, how many megabytes have to be in flight to keep that link full?

In a small office, a ping to the provider takes 15 ms when the line is quiet and 400 ms while the nightly backup uploads, and video calls break up during that time. The manager proposes a plan with twice the bandwidth. What does the lesson recommend instead?

choices.text: The bigger plan: a line twice as wide empties its queue twice as fast
choices.why: A wider line fills more slowly and then builds the same queue; the delay comes back.

choices.text: Shrinking the router's buffer to nothing, so a packet does not wait at all
choices.why: Without a buffer, ordinary bursts turn into losses; the buffer is what stops a burst becoming a loss.

choices.text: Smart queue management, or shaping the line a little under its capacity
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: A bigger jitter buffer in the video app, until the calls stop breaking up
choices.why: A bigger jitter buffer adds its own delay to every word and leaves the 400 ms queue in place.

prompt: The helpdesk log holds four complaints that each say "the internet is slow". Match each one to the number the lesson says it is really about.

pairs.right: bandwidth

pairs.left: Everything feels sluggish, yet files arrive fine
pairs.right: latency

pairs.left: The call breaks only while somebody downloads
pairs.right: queuing

pairs.left: The voice is choppy and keeps cutting out
pairs.right: jitter and loss

prompt: A traceroute to a slow site shows hop 6 at 180 ms, while hops 7 to 11, which lie beyond it, are all around 25 ms. What does the lesson make of hop 6?

choices.text: It is the bottleneck, and the provider that runs it should be called
choices.why: The hops after it would carry its delay too; at 25 ms, the path through hop 6 is fine.

choices.text: Its router answers probes last of all; traffic through it is fine
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: The 180 ms is distance: hop 6 is the first router on another continent
choices.why: A jump caused by distance stays for every hop after it; here it drops back to 25 ms.

choices.text: Its router is overloaded and dropping traffic, which is why the site is slow
choices.why: Traffic crossing it reaches hop 11 in 25 ms; what is slow is the router's own reply to the probe.

prompt: A router's table has three lines: `10.0.0.0 – 10.255.255.255` to router A, `10.20.0.0 – 10.20.255.255` to router B, and everything else to the default gateway. Where does it hand a packet for `10.20.5.9`?

choices.text: To router A, the line that comes first in the table
choices.why: Order does not decide; the most specific matching line wins.

choices.text: To router B
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: To router A, as its line covers more destinations
choices.why: The wider range is the vaguer one; the narrower match wins.

choices.text: To the default gateway, since two lines match it at once
choices.why: The default is for addresses no line covers; this one is covered twice, and the narrower line wins.

prompt: On a lossy Wi-Fi link, a page that loads thirty files over one HTTP/2 connection keeps freezing, then appearing all at once. Which explanation does the lesson give, and what changes it?

choices.text: The MTU is too big for Wi-Fi; HTTP/3 fixes it by sending smaller packets
choices.why: An MTU fault makes large transfers hang outright; HTTP/3's change is recovery per stream.

choices.text: Head-of-line blocking; HTTP/3 resends per stream, so a loss stalls one file
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: UDP is losing the files; moving the page to TCP would resend what is lost
choices.why: HTTP/2 already runs on TCP, and TCP's in-order delivery is what holds the other files back.

choices.text: Bufferbloat in the access point; a larger buffer would smooth the freezes
choices.why: A larger buffer adds delay; stall-then-burst comes from in-order delivery waiting on one lost packet.

prompt: A site renews its certificate automatically using the HTTP check. To tighten things, the network team closed port 80 at the edge, since visitors all use HTTPS. Three months later the certificate expired. What went wrong, and what lets port 80 stay closed?

choices.text: The renewal program waits for a person to approve each renewal, and nobody did
choices.why: The protocol is automatic; it failed because the authority could not reach the site over HTTP.

choices.text: Closing 80 broke the redirect to HTTPS, and sites without one are refused
choices.why: The authority asks for a file on port 80; a redirect is not what it checks.

choices.text: It renewed, but the server still holds the old certificate in memory
choices.why: A real failure elsewhere, but here no renewal happened: the check could not reach port 80.

choices.text: The authority fetches a file over plain HTTP; a DNS check works with 80 shut
choices.why: Right.

prompt: A shop sits behind a CDN that terminates TLS at the edge and talks plain HTTP to the origin. A customer asks whether the padlock means her card number is encrypted all the way to the shop's own server. What is the accurate answer?

choices.text: No: it describes her hop to the edge; the second hop is a setting somebody chose
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Yes: the CDN re-encrypts with the same certificate, so both hops are covered
choices.why: In this arrangement the second hop is plain HTTP; the padlock says nothing about it.

choices.text: Yes: the CDN forwards her encrypted bytes without reading them
choices.why: Terminating means the edge decrypts and opens a second connection; it reads the request.

choices.text: No: TLS protects the address bar, while form fields travel apart
choices.why: Everything in the request shares the encrypted connection to the edge; the gap is the second hop.

prompt: During a traffic spike, `ss -tlnp` on a web server shows the listener on port 443 with `Recv-Q 511` and `Send-Q 511`. What does that pair say?
hint: Linux and the Command Line, lesson 11.

choices.text: 511 bytes are waiting to be acknowledged by clients that went quiet
choices.why: On a LISTEN socket the columns count connections, not bytes; bytes are for established ones.

choices.text: Both queues match, which is the sign that the server is keeping pace
choices.why: Equal means the queue has reached its maximum; that is the overload sign.

choices.text: The backlog is full: the program is slow to accept, and new connections are dropped
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: The network card has run out of descriptors and its driver is behind
choices.why: That is the `missed` counter of `ip -s link`; Recv-Q on a listener is about the program.

prompt: `ip -s link show eth0` has three receive counters that mean trouble. Match each to what the lesson says it points at.
hint: Linux and the Command Line, lesson 11.

pairs.right: a cable or a card: malformed frames, failed checksums
a buffer: the packet was fine and had nowhere to go
the driver: the card had no descriptor free

right_distractors: a firewall rule that discarded the packet

prompt: A cron line pulls every switch's configuration each five minutes. One afternoon the switches answer slowly, a run takes seven minutes, and by evening a dozen copies are fighting over the disk. Which line does the lesson end up with?
hint: Linux and the Command Line, lesson 13.

choices.text: `*/5 * * * * /usr/bin/flock -w 600 /tmp/pull.lock /usr/local/bin/pull.sh`
choices.why: Waiting queues the runs up; a skipped run comes back in five minutes, a queued one is still queued at midnight.

choices.text: `*/5 * * * * /usr/bin/flock -n /tmp/pull.lock /usr/local/bin/pull.sh`
choices.why: Without `-E 0` a busy lock exits 1, and monitoring reports a working job as failed.

choices.text: `*/5 * * * * /usr/bin/flock -E 0 -n /tmp/pull.lock /usr/local/bin/pull.sh`
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: `*/5 * * * * [ -f /tmp/pull.pid ] || /usr/local/bin/pull.sh`, with the script writing its PID
choices.why: Check and write are two steps, and a killed job leaves the file behind, so it stops running for good.

prompt: An Ubuntu server runs in UTC. Its crontab starts with `CRON_TZ=America/Sao_Paulo`, then `0 3 * * * /usr/local/bin/backup.sh`, meant for three in the morning in São Paulo (UTC−3). When does the backup actually run?
hint: Linux and the Command Line, lesson 13.

choices.text: At 03:00 in São Paulo, which is 06:00 UTC
choices.why: On Debian and Ubuntu's cron, CRON_TZ reaches the job as a variable and the scheduler ignores it.

choices.text: At 03:00 UTC, which is midnight in São Paulo
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: It does not run: cron rejects a crontab holding a variable it does not know
choices.why: The variable is accepted and exported into the job; nothing warns you.

choices.text: At 03:00 in the time zone of whoever last edited the crontab
choices.why: Cron uses the machine's zone, from /etc/localtime, not the editor's.

prompt: `switches.txt` lists the management address of each switch, one per line, in no particular order. You suspect two switches were given the same address. Which command names the collisions?
hint: Linux and the Command Line, lesson 8.

choices.text: `sort switches.txt | uniq -d`
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: `uniq -d switches.txt | sort`
choices.why: uniq compares adjacent lines only; unsorted, two equal addresses far apart are missed.

choices.text: `sort -u switches.txt`
choices.why: That prints each address once and throws away the fact that some appeared twice.

choices.text: `sort -n switches.txt | uniq -u`
choices.why: `-u` keeps the lines that appear exactly once, which is the opposite of what you want.

prompt: Plain `sort` prints `1024` before `22` and `443`, because it compares characters rather than values. To order a list of port numbers by value, the command is `sort ___`.
hint: Linux and the Command Line, lesson 8.

prompt: `down=0; cat switches.txt | while read -r ip; do ping -c1 -W1 "$ip" >/dev/null || down=$((down+1)); done; echo "$down down"` prints `0 down`, though two switches are switched off. Why?
hint: Linux and the Command Line, lesson 9.

choices.text: `ping -c1` returns success on a timeout, so the counter stays put
choices.why: ping exits non-zero when no reply comes; the counting happened, in a child process.

choices.text: `$((down+1))` treats `down` as text, so the sum comes out empty
choices.why: Arithmetic expansion reads it as a number; the sum was right inside the subshell.

choices.text: The loop runs in a subshell, so its count is lost when the pipe ends
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: `read -r` stops at the first unreachable address and ends the loop early
choices.why: read stops at end of file; a failing ping does not touch the loop's input.

prompt: `hosts.txt` comes from an inventory tool that leaves no newline after the last line. Which of these loops print every host, the last one included? Choose all that apply.
hint: Linux and the Command Line, lesson 9.

choices.text: `while IFS= read -r h || [ -n "$h" ]; do echo "$h"; done < hosts.txt`
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: `cat hosts.txt | while IFS= read -r h || [ -n "$h" ]; do echo "$h"; done`
choices.why: Right: the subshell loses variables, and printing needs none.

choices.text: `while IFS= read -r h; do echo "$h"; done < hosts.txt`
choices.why: read fails at end of file before a newline, so the last host is read and never printed.

choices.text: `while IFS= read -r h; do echo "$h"; done < <(cat hosts.txt)`
choices.why: Process substitution avoids the subshell, not the missing newline; the last read still fails.

prompt: Before a change window you want to read `firewall.conf` as it was two commits ago, without touching the copy on disk that the deploy script uses. Which command?
hint: Git and Teamwork: Version Control, Review and Process, lesson 4.

choices.text: `git restore --source=HEAD~2 firewall.conf`
choices.why: That writes the old version onto the disk, which is the very file the deploy reads.

choices.text: `git show HEAD~2:firewall.conf`
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: `git reset --soft HEAD~2`
choices.why: That moves the branch back two commits; it rewrites history rather than showing a file.

choices.text: `git revert HEAD~2`
choices.why: That makes a new commit undoing an old one: nothing to read, and something to undo.

prompt: After a bad afternoon in your local repository of switch configurations, which of these can `git reflog` still lead you back to? Choose all that apply.
hint: Git and Teamwork: Version Control, Review and Process, lesson 4.

choices.text: A commit that `git commit --amend` replaced
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Commits that `git reset --hard HEAD~2` stepped past
choices.why: Right: they are on no branch, and still there.

choices.text: A commit on a branch you have since deleted
choices.why: Right: a deleted branch's commits stay findable for weeks.

choices.text: An edit that `git restore` threw away before it was staged
choices.why: It was never committed, so Git never held a copy of it.

choices.text: Uncommitted changes that `git reset --hard` wrote over
choices.why: The reflog keeps commits; what was never committed is gone.

prompt: Git says nothing about `backups/core-sw1.cfg`, though the file is right there. To see which `.gitignore` line hides it: `git ___ -v backups/core-sw1.cfg`.
hint: Git and Teamwork: Version Control, Review and Process, lesson 10.

prompt: The repository's `.gitignore` has `*.cfg`, because configs rendered from templates are rebuilt on every run. One file, `templates/base.cfg`, is written by hand and has to be committed. What do you add?
hint: Git and Teamwork: Version Control, Review and Process, lesson 10.

choices.text: A line `/templates/base.cfg`, which anchors the file to the root
choices.why: A leading slash anchors a pattern; written alone it is one more thing to ignore, not an exception.

choices.text: Nothing: `git add .` picks up ignored files as well
choices.why: `git add .` skips ignored files; keeping them out of it is what ignoring is for.

choices.text: A line `!templates/base.cfg` below the `*.cfg` rule
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: `git rm --cached templates/base.cfg`, so Git tracks it again
choices.why: `rm --cached` stops tracking a file; it is the opposite move.

prompt: Your automation repository holds the templates team's repository as a submodule in `templates/`. They pushed a fix to their `main` yesterday, yet your rendered configs still use the old template, even after `git pull` in your repository. Why?
hint: Git and Teamwork: Version Control, Review and Process, lesson 10.

choices.text: `git pull` skips submodules; `git submodule update --init` brings their latest `main`
choices.why: `update --init` checks out the pinned commit, which is still the old one.

choices.text: The fix is in their history, but Git LFS keeps the old template until it is fetched
choices.why: LFS is about large files; a submodule is pinned to an exact commit.

choices.text: Your project records one commit of theirs and stays on it until somebody moves it and commits
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Their push was refused, as a submodule is read-only to the team that owns it
choices.why: They pushed to their own repository as usual; your project points at an older commit.

prompt: The automation server deploys whichever commit the tag `v2.3` names. You find that `v2.3`, already on the shared copy, was put on the wrong commit. What does the lesson do?
hint: Git and Teamwork: Version Control, Review and Process, lesson 7.

choices.text: Delete `v2.3` and push it again on the right commit, so the name stays tidy
choices.why: People and machines already built from `v2.3`; moving it gives one version number to two commits.

choices.text: Leave `v2.3` alone and tag the right commit `v2.3.1`
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: `git push --force` the right commit, which drags the tag along with it
choices.why: Force moves a branch, and moving a published version is what the lesson rules out.

choices.text: Recreate `v2.3` as a lightweight tag, which is free to point elsewhere
choices.why: Lightweight means fewer details recorded; it is still a fixed name for one commit.

prompt: A colleague pushed a fix to the shared `main` ten minutes ago. On your laptop, `git status` says `Your branch is up to date with 'origin/main'`. What explains it?
hint: Git and Teamwork: Version Control, Review and Process, lesson 7.

choices.text: His push has not reached the server yet; a push takes a few minutes to land
choices.why: A push is complete when it returns; the server already has the commit.

choices.text: He pushed to some other branch, since `status` asks the server about `main`
choices.why: `status` asks nobody; it compares with your bookmark, which moves only on fetch or pull.

choices.text: Your `main` already holds his commit, which Git merged in for you
choices.why: Git does not contact a remote on its own; nothing was merged.

choices.text: `origin/main` is your bookmark from the last fetch, and `git fetch` moves it
choices.why: Right.

prompt: Ticket #41 asks for monitoring on the new switches. For the ticket to be shut automatically when the pull request is merged, its description says `___ #41`, while the commits say `Refs #41`, which only links.
hint: Git and Teamwork: Version Control, Review and Process, lesson 12.

prompt: A cron job asks a network controller's API for the device list every fifteen minutes with `requests.get(url)`. One morning a dozen copies are still running: the controller accepted the connections and then sent nothing. What does the lesson add to that call?

choices.text: `r.raise_for_status()` right after it, so the silence turns into an `HTTPError`
choices.why: raise_for_status reads a status code, and a silent server sends none.

choices.text: `timeout=(3, 10)`, so a silent server raises an exception
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: A `Session`, whose reused connection gives the controller less to stall on
choices.why: A Session saves handshakes; with no timeout it waits on a silent server like any call.

choices.text: A retry adapter for 502, 503 and 504, repeating the call until it answers
choices.why: A retry needs a response or an error to react to; with no timeout the first call does not end.

prompt: A script reaches a controller's API through a `Session` with a retry adapter. By the lesson, which of these responses are worth retrying? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: `429 Too Many Requests`
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: `503 Service Unavailable`
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: `502 Bad Gateway`
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: `404 Not Found`
choices.why: A 404 will say the same thing next time; retrying only repeats it.

choices.text: `400 Bad Request`
choices.why: The request itself is wrong, and it fails the same way however often it is sent.

prompt: `re.findall(r"(\d+)\.(\d+)\.(\d+)\.(\d+)", line)` runs on a log line holding two IPv4 addresses. What does it return?

choices.text: A list of the two addresses, as strings like `'10.0.0.1'`
choices.why: That is findall with no group; with groups it returns the groups, and four of them make tuples.

choices.text: A list of eight strings, the octets one after another
choices.why: With two or more groups each match becomes one tuple; the octets are not flattened.

choices.text: A `Match` for the first address, read with `.group(1)` to `.group(4)`
choices.why: That is what search returns; findall returns every match, in a list.

choices.text: A list of two tuples, each of four strings
choices.why: Right.

prompt: A script flags configuration lines that contain an address the operator types: `re.search(addr, line)` with `addr = "10.0.0.1"`. It also flags lines naming the host `ip-10-0-0-1`. What does the lesson do?

choices.text: Use `re.match`, which compares the whole line instead of searching in it
choices.why: match is anchored at the start only, and its dots still match any character.

choices.text: Add `re.IGNORECASE`, since the host name is written in lower case
choices.why: Case is not the problem; an unescaped dot matches the hyphens.

choices.text: Compile it with `re.compile` first, so that dots are read as dots
choices.why: Compiling names and caches a pattern; it does not change what a dot means.

choices.text: Pass `re.escape(addr)`, so that each dot in it is taken literally
choices.why: Right.

prompt: A nightly job writes the device inventory with `json.dump(data, f, indent=2)` into a file kept in git. Every night the diff shows fields in a different order, although no device changed. The lesson adds `___` to that call.

A collector rewrites `state.json` every minute with `open(path, "w")`, and another process reads that file when it starts. After a power cut, the other process crashes on an empty file. What does the lesson change?

choices.text: Write to `state.tmp` beside it, then `tmp.replace(path)` onto the real name
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Open with `"a"` instead of `"w"`, so the old content stays in place
choices.why: Appending piles each minute's state into one file, which stops being one JSON document.

prompt: In EIGRP, pc2's LAN is cabled to both r2 and r5. r1's best path to it is through r2, with FD 30720; r5 reports a distance of 28160 for the same LAN and would cost r1 33280 in total. What is r5 to r1 for that network?

choices.text: A route r1 has to ask for by going active if r2 fails, as in the ring.

choices.text: A feasible successor, used at once if r2 fails.
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: The pull costs a recalculation within moments; the dead switch costs up to the 40-second dead interval first.

prompt: A small company with two providers must never carry traffic between them. Which measures stand in the way of that route leak? Choose all that apply.

choices.why: A longer path makes the leak less attractive where nothing outranks length, which real local preference does.

prompt: An analyser on a 1 Gbit/s mirror port captures a busy 10 Gbit/s uplink. The capture has gaps in TCP streams that the two ends never retransmitted. What is the likeliest explanation?

prompt: Two shops are both numbered 192.168.20.0/24, and on hq each is a WireGuard peer with `AllowedIPs = 192.168.20.0/24`. What happens?

choices.why: An outgoing packet needs exactly one answer to which key encrypts it.

choices.text: hq refuses the second peer with an error naming the overlap.
choices.why: Nothing refuses it: giving the range to a second peer silently takes it from the first.

choices.text: The range moves to the peer configured last, and only that shop is reached.
choices.why: Right.

choices.why: Half-open handshakes are a TCP SYN flood; the questions here are small UDP packets.

choices.text: Strangers use it to aim amplified replies at a victim whose address they forge.
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Anybody can read the company's internal names from it, which helps an intruder plan where to go next.
choices.why: The risk the lesson names is to others: the server becomes a reflector in somebody else's attack.

choices.why: Load is not the concern; being used to flood a third party is.

choices.why: Right.

choices.why: That acts on what arrives; the forged questions leave the network untouched.

choices.why: SYN cookies help a server under a SYN flood; they do nothing about what leaves.

choices.why: A per-source limit tames one noisy client arriving; it does not check outgoing sources.

choices.text: In a `job` label, which Prometheus adds anyway.

prompt: A host that runs an exporter loses power. Because Prometheus pulls, it notices: the scrape fails, and a metric Prometheus keeps for every target, 1 or 0 on every scrape, drops to 0. That metric is called ___.
Put the moments of an incident in the order its intervals are measured between.
trap: Mitigation comes before closing: users stop being hurt by the rollback, and the incident is closed later.

prompt: During an incident, one role records what is tried, decided and observed, with times, and does nothing else. That role is the ___.

A network team puts a new reverse proxy between `storefront` and `orders` that forwards only a fixed list of headers. From that day every checkout shows up in Jaeger as two separate traces. What is the likeliest cause?

choices.text: The proxy adds latency, and Jaeger splits a trace whose spans are too far apart in time.
choices.why: Spans join by ids, not by how close they are in time.

choices.text: `orders` now sees the proxy as its caller and records it as the root.
choices.why: The proxy creates no span here; what is missing is the context the proxy dropped.

choices.text: The proxy rewrites the third field of the header with its own span id.
choices.why: Rewriting the parent field would still keep the trace id, so the trace would stay one.

choices.text: `traceparent` is not on the list, so `orders` starts a new trace.
choices.why: Right.

prompt: At three in the morning nobody is buying, and the checkout path is broken. Why can the burn-rate page not fire, and what does lesson 16 rely on instead?

choices.text: The burn rate ignores traffic, so it fires as usual and nothing else is needed.
choices.why: It ignores the volume, but with no requests the ratio has nothing to divide.

choices.text: Alertmanager mutes pages at night unless a silence is lifted.
choices.why: Silences are added by people for a window; nothing mutes pages by the clock.

choices.text: The one-hour window is still full of daytime requests, which dilute the failures.
choices.why: At three in the morning the last hour holds no daytime traffic; the problem is that it holds none.

choices.text: Nothing over nothing is undefined; a failing synthetic checkout is the signal.
choices.why: Right.

prompt: Two outages of the same length hit the same shop: one at four in the morning, one at lunchtime. How do they compare against the error budget?

choices.text: The midday one costs far more, since failed checkouts are what is counted.
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: They spend the same, because the budget is a number of minutes per window.
choices.why: The budget is counted in failed checkouts, and the minutes are only a way of picturing it.

choices.text: The night one spends more, since fewer requests make each failure a bigger share.
choices.why: The budget is a share of all checkouts in the window, and the night outage fails far fewer of them.

choices.text: Neither counts, as an outage is excluded from the SLI.
choices.why: An outage is exactly what the SLI measures.

prompt: A firewall change cuts three replicas off from their database for five minutes. Their liveness probe opens a TCP connection to `db:5432`. Which of these happen? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: Every replica is restarted, at about the same moment, more than once.
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Requests in flight are dropped at each restart.
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Kubernetes waits longer between restarts each time, which delays recovery once the database returns.
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: The restarts reconnect the replicas to the database sooner than waiting would.
choices.why: A restart cannot bring the network path or the database back.

choices.text: Traffic moves to the healthy replicas while the others restart.
choices.why: All three fail the same probe at once, so there is no healthy replica to move to.

prompt: Before sending support tickets to a model, a script applies lesson 11's patterns, including `(?:\d[ -]?){13,19}` for cards. A ticket carries a card written `4111.1111.1111.1111`. What happens?

choices.text: It leaves with the request: a pattern catches formats, not meaning.
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: It is replaced by `[CARD]`, since the pattern counts digits whatever separates them.
choices.why: The pattern allows a space or a hyphen between digits, not a dot.

choices.text: The provider refuses the request, because card numbers are blocked at the API.
choices.why: The lesson's own log shows the provider receiving the number when nothing removed it.

choices.text: The `SECRET` pattern catches it instead.
choices.why: That pattern looks for words such as token or password followed by a value.

prompt: A team builds an agent for network operations with three tools: read an interface's counters, read a device's configuration, and push a configuration. Which arrangements follow lesson 7's rules? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: The host asks a person before the push, showing the exact arguments.
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: The agent runs with credentials of its own, scoped to what its tools need.
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Every call and every result is logged, with who approved what.
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: The system prompt tells the model never to push without approval, so the host need not check.
choices.why: Limits are enforced below the model, where its choices cannot reach.

choices.text: The agent borrows the engineer's own session, which already has the right access.
choices.why: The lesson says the agent's own credentials, never the developer's.

prompt: A model drafts replies to customers' tickets, and the host offers it every tool the application has, including one that issues refunds. Which change holds however a ticket is worded?

choices.text: A sentence in the system prompt telling the model to ignore instructions found inside tickets.
choices.why: That asks the model to behave; the lesson's first version had exactly that and still paid.

choices.text: A filter that deletes phrases like "ignore previous instructions" before the request.
choices.why: It depends on the wording, which is the property the question rules out.

choices.text: A larger model, which follows its instructions better.
choices.why: No model can be relied on to ignore instructions in the data.

choices.text: Offer the drafting task only the tools that read.
choices.why: Right.

prompt: A script wraps the SDK call in its own loop that retries any exception five times. One request keeps failing with 400. What does lesson 10 say is wrong?

choices.text: The loop retries what time cannot fix, and multiplies the SDK's own waits on top.
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Five is too few; a 400 clears once the provider's load drops.
choices.why: Overload is 529 or 5xx; a 400 is a request that is wrong and will be wrong again.

choices.text: The loop should honour `retry-after`, which every 400 carries.
choices.why: `retry-after` comes with a 429, a rate limit; it says nothing about a malformed request.

choices.text: Nothing, as long as the waits grow with jitter.
choices.why: Backoff spaces retries out; it does not make a wrong request right.

prompt: The SDKs wait longer before each retry and add a random part, so that two clients that failed together do not retry together. That is exponential backoff with ___.
`ansible-playbook` fails on a router task, and an engineer asks an assistant for help. By lesson 5, which of these belong in the request? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: The command that produced the failure.
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: The error and the traceback, unedited.
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: The versions involved, and what was already tried.
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: A summary of the error in the engineer's own words instead of the error itself.
choices.why: A description makes the model guess; the evidence carries details nobody thinks to mention.

choices.text: The router's enable password, so the model can reproduce the session.
choices.why: Secrets stay out of a prompt; the model needs the error, not the credentials.

prompt: An assistant writes a Terraform block using an argument the provider removed in a release after the model's training cutoff. What does lesson 1 recommend?

choices.text: Put the docs of the version in use into the context, and check the result against something that is not a model.
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Ask the model whether it is sure, since a large model can say "I don't know".
choices.why: That is a learnt behaviour, not a measurement; the model has no signal for what it is reconstructing.

choices.text: Lower the temperature to 0, so the answer is the most likely and so the correct one.
choices.why: The most likely continuation of old training text is still the old argument.

choices.text: Switch to a provider whose model knows Terraform.
choices.why: Any model has a cutoff, and this argument changed after it.

By lesson 3, which of these make a strong portfolio project for somebody hiring a junior network engineer? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: A lab network built from configuration files kept under version control.
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: A topology diagram of that lab.
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: A test that proves the lab fails over when a link goes down.
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: A list of the courses and certificates finished, at the top of the README.

prompt: Your lab's failover test has passed on every run since you wrote it, after the redundancy was already in place. How does lesson 12 say to find out whether it would notice a broken failover?
hint: The Portfolio Project: From Brief to Deploy, lesson 12.

choices.text: Run it on every push, so a failure would show up as a red cross.
choices.why: Running it more often does not show that it can fail at all.

choices.text: Add more tests around it until coverage of the configuration reaches a high percentage.
choices.why: Coverage counts lines run, not whether this test objects when the guarantee is gone.

choices.text: Read it again the next morning.
choices.why: Distance helps a review; it does not prove the test bites.

choices.text: Remove the redundant path on purpose, watch the test go red, then restore it.
choices.why: Right.

prompt: You plan a lab network with three segments, routing between them, monitoring and a failover test. What does lesson 5's walking skeleton say to have working in the first days?
hint: The Portfolio Project: From Brief to Deploy, lesson 5.

choices.text: Every segment fully designed and documented, so that nothing has to be redone later.
choices.why: That is the layer-by-layer route, where nothing runs until the last layer is done.

choices.text: The monitoring stack, since it will show every later problem.
choices.why: One layer done first is still a layer; the skeleton is a slice through all of them.

choices.text: The thinnest slice end to end: two segments that reach each other, built from the files in the repository, with no polish yet.
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: The failover test, written before any device exists.
choices.why: Tests come after something works, in the skeleton's order.

prompt: Six weeks are not enough for your network lab project's plan: a web dashboard with accounts and roles, the failover test, a diagram and a README. By lesson 6, what goes first?
hint: The Portfolio Project: From Brief to Deploy, lesson 6.

choices.text: The diagram, which a reviewer can draw from the configurations.
choices.why: The diagram is the first thing this field's reviewer opens.

choices.text: The failover test, the largest single piece of work.
choices.why: It is the project's point, and the point is never on the cutting list.

choices.text: The sign-in and permissions, since every screen and test multiplies by them.
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: The README, which can be written after the deadline.
choices.why: The README is what gets the project understood; cutting it hides the work.

prompt: On the networks track, what does lesson 15 say "deployed" means for your project?
hint: The Portfolio Project: From Brief to Deploy, lesson 15.

choices.text: It ran once from start to finish on your own laptop, recorded in a screenshot.
choices.why: Deployed means somebody can see it working without you, next month as well as today.

choices.text: An environment that keeps running, is documented well enough to rebuild, and has a restore that was tested.
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Reachable from the internet under a domain of its own.
choices.why: The course's own deploy is on a private lab network; a domain is not the test.

choices.text: Merged to main with a green CI run.
choices.why: A green run says the tests passed, not that anything is up for somebody else.

prompt: Your lab project includes a small tool that hands out subnets and refuses one that overlaps a subnet already given. Which test earns its keep, by lesson 12?

choices.text: One that checks Python's `ipaddress` parses `10.0.16.0/20` correctly.
choices.why: The library has its own tests; this one proves nothing about your rule.

choices.text: A test for the rule at its edge: a block sharing one address is refused, and the block right after it is accepted.
choices.why: Right.
